source_refs.note: Chapter 5 exercise as printed (PDF 150-152, printed 147-149), each question with its solution. MCQ answers follow the chapter's text; where the answer key (PDF 226) differs, a Book correction box follows the question.

blocks.prompt: 1. Which of the following is an example of a basic statistical model?
blocks.explanation: Linear regression is the basic statistical model of the chapter (5.4.1.2): it fits a straight line Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε to predict one variable from another. Neural networks, decision trees and support vector machines are advanced machine-learning methods.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key at the end of the book (Unit 5) gives (b). Neural networks are not a basic statistical model and are not taught in the chapter; the chapter's basic models are linear and logistic regression (5.4.1.1-5.4.1.3), so the answer is (a).

blocks.prompt: 2. What does experimental design in data science involve?
blocks.explanation: Experimental design means planning how data will be collected and analysed in a systematic, controlled way: one variable is changed and its effect on another is measured (5.3.1.3), e.g. comparing two groups of students with and without printed notes.

blocks.prompt: 3. Which of the following is NOT a type of data visualization?
blocks.explanation: A hypothesis test is a statistical method for checking a claim with data; it is not a chart. Bar charts and scatter plots are types of visualization in 5.5.1, and a heatmap shows values with colours.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key at the end of the book (Unit 5) gives (b). A scatter plot is itself a type of visualization (5.5.1.4, Figure 5.7). The option that is not a visualization is (c) Hypothesis Test.

blocks.prompt: 4. Which tool is commonly used for creating data visualizations?
blocks.explanation: The chapter names MS Excel, Google Sheets, Python, Tableau and Matplotlib as data visualization software (learning outcomes, 5.6), so all of the above are commonly used.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key at the end of the book (Unit 5) gives (a). MS Excel is only one of the tools; Python (Matplotlib) and Tableau are also named in the chapter, so the complete answer is (d) All of the above.

blocks.prompt: 5. What does the slope in a linear regression model represent?

options.text: The change in the dependent variable for a unit change in the independent variable

blocks.explanation: The slope β₁ shows how much Y changes with each unit increase in X (5.4.1.2). In the fruit-stall model β₁ = 40: each extra customer adds 40 rupees.

blocks.prompt: 6. Which of the following is an example of a real-world application of statistical models?
blocks.explanation: Statistical models are used to make predictions from data (5.1.3, 5.4.1); predicting house prices from size, location and similar data is such an application. The other options are creative tasks, not predictions from data.

blocks.prompt: 7. Which of the following is NOT a benefit of data visualization?
blocks.explanation: Visualization turns numbers into easy-to-understand charts (5.5, 5.6); it makes data simpler, not more complex. Spotting trends, communicating insights and summarizing large data are its benefits.

blocks.prompt: 8. What is the primary goal of K-Means Clustering?

options.text: To classify data into predefined categories
To group data into clusters based on similarity
To reduce the dimensionality of data

blocks.explanation: Clustering groups similar things together based on their characteristics (5.4.1.4); K-means places each point in the cluster with the nearest centre, e.g. math-strong and English-strong students.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key at the end of the book (Unit 5) gives (a). Putting data into predefined categories is classification, which needs labelled categories in advance. K-means has no predefined labels; it forms groups by similarity (5.4.1.4), so the answer is (b).

blocks.prompt: 9. In K-Means Clustering, what does the "K" represent?

options.text: The number of features in the dataset
The number of clusters to be formed
The number of iterations required for convergence
The number of data points in the dataset

blocks.explanation: K is the number of clusters (groups) we decide to form; it is chosen in Step 1 (5.4.1.4). In the student example K = 2.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key at the end of the book (Unit 5) gives (c). The number of iterations is not fixed in advance; K-means repeats until the centres stop moving. K is the number of clusters chosen in Step 1 (5.4.1.4), so the answer is (b). The key also prints a tenth answer, (a), although the exercise has only nine MCQs.

blocks.prompt: 1. What is the importance of building statistical models in real-world applications?
blocks.explanation:
A statistical model uses data to make sense of a situation and predict what will happen (5.4.1). Its importance:
- Simplifies complex problems by keeping the important factors and leaving out unnecessary details (5.1.1).
- Shows how variables are related, e.g. customers and earnings.
- Predicts future outcomes, such as weather, prices or exam results.
- Supports better decisions by comparing outcomes before acting (5.1.2), e.g. a farmer choosing the best planting time.
- Is used in many fields: weather forecasting, financial predictions and scientific research (5.1.3).

blocks.prompt: 2. Name one basic statistical model used for predicting outcomes and explain its purpose.
blocks.explanation:
Linear regression (5.4.1.2).
Purpose: it finds the straight-line relationship between an independent variable X (the cause) and a dependent variable Y (the effect), so that Y can be predicted from X.
Formula: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε, where β₀ is the intercept (Y when X = 0), β₁ the slope (change in Y per unit of X) and ε the error term.
Example: a fruit stall's model Earnings = 100 + 40 x Customers predicts that 22 customers give 100 + 40 x 22 = 980 rupees.

blocks.prompt: 3. List two types of data visualizations and describe when you would use each.
blocks.explanation:
1. Bar chart: used to compare different categories. Each bar is a category and its height shows the value. Use it, for example, to compare the sales of different products in a store (5.5.1.1).
2. Line graph: used to show trends over time. Data points are joined by a line, so rises and falls are easy to see. Use it, for example, to show how the temperature changes during a day or week (5.5.1.2).
(Others: a histogram for the distribution of exam scores, a scatterplot for the relation between hours studied and scores.)

blocks.prompt: 4. How does visualizing data help in understanding descriptive statistics?
blocks.explanation:
Descriptive statistics summarize data with numbers such as the mean, median, mode, range, variance and standard deviation (5.2). Visualizing the same data makes these summaries easy to see at a glance:
- A histogram shows where most values lie and how spread out they are (distribution).
- A boxplot shows the median, quartiles and outliers, and compares the spread of groups (e.g. classes).
- Bar and line charts compare averages or show trends over time.
- Patterns, unusual values and differences in spread (such as Class A's variance 12.56 against Class B's 454) are noticed without reading every number.

blocks.prompt: 5. What is the purpose of using tools like MS Excel for data visualization?
blocks.explanation:
Tools like MS Excel and Google Sheets let anyone turn data into charts easily (5.6, 5.6.1):
- Data is entered in rows and columns, and a bar chart, line graph or pie chart is made with a few clicks (Insert tab), without programming.
- Charts can be customized with titles and axis labels, which makes them easier to interpret.
- The tools are widely available and familiar, so results are quick to make and share.
Example: a small business enters monthly sales in Excel and makes a bar chart to see which month had the most sales.

blocks.prompt: 6. Give an example of a real-world problem where a statistical model could be applied.
blocks.explanation:
Predicting the daily earnings of a fruit stall (5.4.1.2).
- Problem: the owner wants to know how much he will earn tomorrow.
- Data: number of customers (X) and daily earnings (Y) for past days.
- Model: linear regression gives Earnings = 100 + 40 x Customers.
- Use: if 22 customers are expected, predicted earnings = 980 rupees, which helps in buying stock.
Other examples: predicting house prices, forecasting weather, a farmer choosing the planting time, or predicting whether a student will pass from study hours (logistic regression).

blocks.prompt: 1. Explain the role and importance of statistical models in solving real-world problems.
blocks.explanation:
Statistical model: a simplified representation of a real situation, built from data, that helps us understand, explain or predict how things work (5.1.1, 5.4.1). Like a map that shows only roads and landmarks, it keeps the important factors and leaves out unnecessary details.
Role in solving problems:
1. Understanding: it shows how variables are related, e.g. how the number of customers affects earnings.
2. Prediction: it estimates future outcomes from past data, e.g. next month's grocery expenses or tomorrow's earnings.
3. Decision-making: it gives a structured way to think and lets us compare outcomes before choosing (5.1.2). A farmer uses weather and soil data to choose the best planting time.
4. Measuring reliability: testing on new data shows the error, so we know how far to trust a prediction.
Importance in real-world fields (5.1.3):
- Weather forecasting: temperature, humidity and wind speed data are analysed to forecast the weather.
- Financial predictions: banks and companies predict economic trends, stock prices and customer behaviour.
- Scientific research: scientists test theories and make predictions; with ML and AI, models analyse large data more accurately.
- Education and business: predicting exam results from study hours, or grouping customers with clustering.
Care needed: models must be fair (not biased against any group) and must respect data privacy (5.4.2.3).
Conclusion: statistical models turn data into understanding and predictions, which leads to better, evidence-based decisions.

blocks.prompt: 2. Describe the steps involved in building a basic statistical model (e.g., linear regression). Include details on data collection, model training, and evaluation.
blocks.explanation:
Building a statistical model has five steps (5.4.1.1). Example: predicting a fruit stall's daily earnings from the number of customers with linear regression (5.4.1.2).
Step 1: Define the problem
- Decide what to predict and which factors affect it. Here Y = daily earnings (dependent variable) and X = number of customers (independent variable).
Step 2: Collect data
- Gather past data on the problem: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 customers gave 500, 700, 900, 1,100, 1,300 rupees.
- Prepare it: clean errors, handle missing values and remove duplicates (5.3.2, 5.3.3).
Step 3: Choose an algorithm
- The relationship looks like a straight line, so choose linear regression: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε.
Step 4: Train the model
- The model learns β₀ and β₁ from the data.
- Slope: every 5 extra customers add 200 rupees, so β₁ = 200/5 = 40.
- Intercept: 500 = β₀ + 40 x 10, so β₀ = 500 - 400 = 100.
- Model: Earnings = 100 + 40 x Customers.
- Use: for 22 customers, Earnings = 100 + 40 x 22 = 980 rupees.
Step 5: Evaluate the model
- Test it on new data it has not seen. On day 6, 28 customers came and 1,250 rupees were earned.
- Predicted = 100 + 40 x 28 = 1,220 rupees; Error = 1,220 - 1,250 = -30 rupees.
- A small error means the model predicts well; error metrics (and accuracy metrics for yes/no models) measure performance (5.4.2.1).
- If the error is large, use more data or more factors and update the model regularly.

blocks.prompt: 3. Discuss the types of data visualizations and their uses.
blocks.explanation:
Data visualization is the process of representing data in a visual format such as graphs or charts, so that patterns, trends and insights are grasped quickly (5.5). Common types (5.5.1):
1. Bar charts
- Compare different categories; each bar is a category and its height (or length) shows the value.
- Use: comparing the sales of different products in a store (Figure 5.4).
2. Line graphs
- Show trends over time by joining data points with a line.
- Use: tracking temperature rising and falling during a day or week (Figure 5.5), or sales over months.
3. Histograms
- Show the distribution of a dataset by grouping values into bins (intervals) and showing how often values fall in each.
- Use: the distribution of students' maths exam scores (Figure 5.6).
4. Scatterplots
- Show the relationship between two variables; each point is one observation.
- Use: hours studied against exam scores (Figure 5.7); a rising pattern shows that more study goes with higher scores.
5. Boxplots (whisker plots)
- Summarize a distribution with the median, quartiles and possible outliers, showing variability.
- Use: comparing the exam scores of different classes (Figure 5.8).
Others named in the chapter: pie charts (parts of a whole) and heatmaps (values shown by colour).
Tools: MS Excel, Google Sheets, Python (Matplotlib) and Tableau (5.6).
Uses of visualization in general: identifying trends and patterns, communicating insights effectively and summarizing large datasets.

blocks.prompt: 4. Explain the concept of model evaluation in statistical modeling.
blocks.explanation:
Model evaluation: after a model is built, it is checked to see how well it performs and what its results mean (5.4.2). It is the last step of model development: the model is tested with new data to ensure it makes good predictions (5.4.1.1).
1. Testing on new data
- The model is used on data it was not trained on, and its predictions are compared with the actual values.
2. Performance metrics (5.4.2.1)
- Error metrics measure how far predictions are from actual values. Grocery example: predicted 8,000 rupees, actual 10,000 rupees, error 2,000 rupees. Fruit-stall example: predicted 1,220, actual 1,250, error -30 rupees.
- Accuracy metrics measure how many predictions were correct, e.g. how often a pass/fail model was right (if 8 of 10 predictions are correct, accuracy = 8/10 = 80%).
3. Interpreting outputs (5.4.2.2)
- Understanding what the results tell us and drawing conclusions, e.g. if hours studied strongly affect scores, students should study more hours.
4. Ethical considerations (5.4.2.3)
- Fairness: the model should not favour one group unfairly (e.g. in loan decisions).
- Privacy: personal data must be kept secure and not shared without permission.
5. Improving the model
- If performance is poor: use more data, include relevant factors, update the model with new data and keep testing predictions against actual values.
Importance: evaluation shows whether a model's predictions can be trusted before it is used for real decisions.

blocks.prompt: 5. Explain the K-Means Clustering algorithm step by step. Include details on how initial centroids are selected, how data points are assigned to clusters, and how centroids are updated.
blocks.explanation:
K-means clustering groups similar data points into K clusters; each cluster has a centre (centroid), and each point belongs to the cluster with the nearest centroid (5.4.1.4).
Example data (math, English scores): Basim (85, 70), Umer (90, 65), Anie (50, 80), Tallat (40, 85), Maliha (60, 60).
Step 1: Select the number of clusters K
- Decide how many groups are wanted. Here K = 2 (math-strong and English-strong students).
Step 2: Select the initial centroids
- Choose K starting centres, usually K data points picked at random.
- Here: Centre 1 = Basim (85, 70), Centre 2 = Tallat (40, 85).
Step 3: Assign each point to the nearest centroid
- Find each point's distance to every centre with the Euclidean distance: Distance = √((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²).
- Basim: 0 and 47.43; Umer: 7.07 and 53.85; Anie: 36.40 and 11.18; Tallat: 47.43 and 0; Maliha: 26.93 and 32.02.
- Each point joins the nearer centre: Cluster 1 = Basim, Umer, Maliha; Cluster 2 = Anie, Tallat.
Step 4: Update (recalculate) the centroids
- Each new centroid is the average of the points in its cluster.
- Centre 1 = ((85 + 90 + 60)/3, (70 + 65 + 60)/3) = (78.33, 65); Centre 2 = ((50 + 40)/2, (80 + 85)/2) = (45, 82.5).
Step 5: Repeat Steps 3 and 4 until the centroids stop moving
- With the new centres, Maliha is 19.00 from Centre 1 and 27.04 from Centre 2, and no student changes cluster, so the centroids no longer change and the clusters are stable (convergence).
Result: Cluster 1 = Basim, Umer, Maliha (good in math); Cluster 2 = Anie, Tallat (good in English).
(In the book's worked example Maliha is first put in Cluster 2, but its own distances, 26.92 against 32.02, place her in Cluster 1; the final result is the same.)

blocks.prompt: 6. Describe a real-world scenario where K-Means Clustering can be applied. Explain how you would preprocess the data, choose the value of K, and interpret the results.
blocks.explanation:
Scenario: customer segmentation in a local retail shop (the chapter's K-means class activity). The shop wants to group customers by their monthly spending on groceries and clothing, so it can plan offers for each group.
Data ($ groceries, $ clothing): C1 (150, 100), C2 (200, 150), C3 (100, 50), C4 (80, 20), C5 (160, 90), C6 (40, 10).
1. Preprocessing the data
- Collect the spending records for each customer (e.g. from sales records).
- Clean the data: correct wrong entries, remove duplicate customers, and handle missing values by removing, flagging or filling them with an average (5.3.3).
- Keep the same units (dollars per month) for both features; if features have very different ranges, scale them so that one feature does not dominate the distance.
2. Choosing K
- Choose K from the business need: the shop wants two groups (high spenders and low spenders), so K = 2.
- In general, try a few values of K and choose the one that gives clear, well-separated and useful groups.
3. Running K-means
- Initial centres (chosen from the data): C2 (200, 150) and C6 (40, 10).
- Distances to the two centres: C1 70.71 / 142.13; C2 0 / 212.60; C3 141.42 / 72.11; C4 176.92 / 41.23; C5 72.11 / 144.22; C6 212.60 / 0.
- Clusters: Cluster 1 = C1, C2, C5; Cluster 2 = C3, C4, C6.
- New centres (averages): Cluster 1 = (170, 113.33); Cluster 2 = (73.33, 26.67).
- Repeat: distances to the new centres are C1 24.04 / 106.09, C2 47.38 / 176.79, C3 94.40 / 35.43, C4 129.66 / 9.43, C5 25.39 / 107.34, C6 166.07 / 37.27; nobody changes cluster, so the centres are stable.
4. Interpreting the results
- Cluster 1 (C1, C2, C5): high spenders, about $170 on groceries and $113 on clothing per month. The shop can offer them loyalty rewards and new or premium clothing.
- Cluster 2 (C3, C4, C6): low spenders, about $73 on groceries and $27 on clothing. The shop can attract them with discounts and grocery deals.
- The results are checked with new data over time and the clusters are updated when spending habits change.
